title: Reading files: whole file vs streaming
summary: Use os.ReadFile when the file comfortably fits in memory; stream it with bufio.Scanner when it might not, or when one pass is all you need.

examples.title: Read the whole file with os.ReadFile

annotations.note: One call opens, reads and closes the file. The error is an ordinary return value: nothing forces you to check it, but ignoring it is a bug.
string(data) copies the bytes. That's fine for a config file. For a 500 MB export it doubles memory, which is the cue to stream instead.

examples.title: Stream line by line with bufio.Scanner

annotations.note: defer schedules f.Close() for when main returns, on every return path. But log.Fatalf calls os.Exit, which skips deferred calls: harmless in a tiny program, a real bug in a server.
Memory use stays constant no matter how big the file is: one line at a time.
Scan returns false both at end of file and on error. Only sc.Err() tells the two apart, so this check isn't optional.
Go randomizes map iteration order on purpose. slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) (iterators, Go 1.23) gives stable output.

use_cases: os.ReadFile: config files, small JSON/CSV, templates, test fixtures
bufio.Scanner: logs, large CSV exports, uploaded files, anything of unknown size
strengths: os.ReadFile is one call and closes the file for you; there's no resource to leak
Scanner uses constant memory regardless of file size
Both build on io.Reader, so the same scanning code works on files, network connections, gzip streams and HTTP bodies, without Java's InputStream class hierarchy
weaknesses: os.ReadFile holds the whole file in memory, and converting to string copies it again
Scanner's default maximum token size is 64 KB; longer lines stop the scan with bufio.ErrTooLong
Errors have to be checked in two places: at Open and after the loop

pitfalls.title: Skipping sc.Err()
pitfalls.detail: A too-long line ends the loop early and looks like EOF. Always check sc.Err(); raise the limit with sc.Buffer(...) if you need to.

pitfalls.title: Relative paths resolve against the working directory
pitfalls.detail: They don't resolve against the source file. In servers, resolve paths from configuration.

pitfalls.title: Untrusted file names can escape a directory
pitfalls.detail: "../../etc/passwd". Use os.Root (Go 1.24) or filepath.IsLocal before opening user-supplied paths.

quiz.q: sc.Scan() returned false. What do you know?
quiz.why: Scan reports false for both EOF and errors; Err() returns nil only at a clean EOF.

quiz.q: You must read a 2 GB CSV on a 4 GB machine. Which do you reach for?
quiz.why: os.ReadFile would need the file (plus its string copy) in memory; Scanner holds one line.

body:
## Concept

Go gives you two levels of file reading. `os.ReadFile` returns the whole content as
`[]byte`. `os.Open` returns an `*os.File`, which is an `io.Reader`, and you consume it
piece by piece, usually through `bufio.Scanner` (line by line) or `bufio.Reader`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Python: `Path.read_text()` ≈ `os.ReadFile`; `for line in f:` ≈ the `Scanner` loop.
- Java: `Files.readAllBytes` vs `BufferedReader.lines()`. There are no checked exceptions:
  errors are return values, and linters (`errcheck`) catch the ones you ignore.
- C: a `fgets` loop without buffer overflows. An over-long line becomes an error, not memory corruption.
- Node: `fs.readFileSync` vs `readline` over a stream. Go's version is synchronous code
  that doesn't block other goroutines.

## Design notes

Accept an `io.Reader`, not a file name: `func countLevels(r io.Reader) (map[string]int, error)`.
Opening the file stays at the edge of the program (`main`, an HTTP handler), and the logic
works on files, request bodies, gzip streams and `strings.NewReader` in tests. This is Go's
everyday form of dependency inversion, and it's why `io.Reader` is the most important
interface in the standard library. The exercise has you do exactly this refactor.
